question.knowledge_point: Finding the Derivative of a Polar Curve Given the Derivatives With Respect To X and Y
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14059545/assets/dcb8b5dee06f59322f2f365512065857c79715be39f96a50d91cc9062991aa6e.png)

Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the polar curve $r=10{e}^{-\theta }$ (shown above) given that

$$
{y}^{′}(\theta )=10{e}^{-\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ),\,{x}^{′}(\theta )=-10{e}^{-\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).
$$
question.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ we use the rule

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{10{e}^{-\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}{-10{e}^{-\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Derivative of a Polar Curve at a Point Given Derivatives With Respect To X and Y
question.problem:
Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the polar curve $r=2\theta $  at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$ given that

$$
{y}^{′}(\theta )=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,{x}^{′}(\theta )=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$
question.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ we use the rule

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}.
$$

We have,

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}+2(\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =2+0 \\  & =2,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}-2(\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =0-\pi  \\  & =-\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =\pi /2} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})}{{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})} \\  & =\frac{2}{-\pi } \\  & =-\frac{2}{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Derivative of a Constant Polar Curve
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14059545/assets/40375a9794d9e399327cfcf128e017f05d20319fd86d41a8a9f49e01f58ccae0.png)

Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the polar curve $r=4$  (shown above) at $\theta =\frac{7\pi }{4}.$
question.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}
$$

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Using the fact that $r=4,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\ =-\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =7\pi /4} & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{4}) \\  & =-(-1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Determining the Image of an Object Formed by a Singular Transformation
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14059760/assets/0cec723bf4e6886ca0715e9e02c658a7ee0e1f24555ea3946f95aa2b12b863be.png)

Consider the linear transformation $T$ with matrix representation $T,$ given by

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Which of the following is the image of the triangle shown above under the action of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
To find the image of the triangle under the action of $T$, we first create a matrix $X$ containing all of the vertices of the triangle:

$$
X=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute the image of $X$ under the action of $T$ by calculating the matrix product $TX:$

$$
\begin{aligned}TX & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the image's vertices are $(-2,2)$, $(-2,2),$ $(2,-2).$ Notice that all three points lie on the same line.

So, the image of our triangle under the action of $T$ is as follows:

question.knowledge_point: Writing a Complex Number Shown on an Argand Diagram in Exponential Form
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14059847/assets/83c490278bec718da1338f8926e9d67d2f72909487b9a85bbd386cbf72def2bb.png)

Write the complex number $z$, shown on the Argand diagram above, in the form $r{e}^{\text{i}\theta },$ giving $\theta $ in radians to $3$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
The complex number shown in the Argand diagram can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =x+\text{i}y \\  & =-4+\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

To write it in the form $z=r{\text{e}}^{\text{i}\theta },$ where $r=|z|$ and $\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z),$ we first calculate $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-4)^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{17}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $z$ lies in the second quadrant of the complex plane, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\pi -|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})| \\  & =\pi -|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-\frac{1}{4})| \\  & ≈2.897.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $r=\sqrt{17}$ and $\theta =2.897$ into $z=r{e}^{\text{i}\theta },$ we get

$$
z=\sqrt{17}\,{\text{e}}^{2.897\,\text{i}}.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Writing a Complex Number in Exponential Form
question.problem: Write the complex number $z=-2+6\text{i}$ in the form $r{e}^{\text{i}\theta },$ giving $\theta $ in radians to $3$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
To write our complex number in the form $z=r{\text{e}}^{\text{i}\theta },$ where $r=|z|$ and $\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z),$ we first calculate $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{6}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $z$ lies in the second quadrant of the complex plane, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\pi -|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})| \\  & =\pi -|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-3)| \\  & ≈1.893.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $r=2\sqrt{10}$ and $\theta =1.893$ into $z=r{e}^{\text{i}\theta },$ we get

$$
z=2\sqrt{10}\,{\text{e}}^{1.893\,\text{i}}.
$$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Which of the following is the image of the triangle shown above under the action of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
To find the image of the triangle under the action of $T$, we first create a matrix $X$ containing all of the vertices of the triangle:

$$
X=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute the image of $X$ under the action of $T$ by calculating the matrix product $TX:$

$$
\begin{aligned}TX & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 & 2 \\ 4 & 20 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

question.knowledge_point: Identifying the Type of Image Formed by a Linear Transformation
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14060375/assets/e2ab6906100a96a123b4b1520613f1e38fe2c7e77af390a8efe0596a2861727d.png)

Consider the linear transformation $T$ with matrix representation $T,$ given by

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

What would be the image of the triangle shown above under the action of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that for any linear transformation $T$ with associated $2\times 2$ matrix $T,$ we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $T$ is non-singular, i.e., $det(T)\ne 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $T$ is singular, i.e., $det(T)=0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $T$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $T$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is the point $(0,0),$ the origin of the coordinate system.

Since $T$ is the zero matrix, the image of our object under the action of $T$ is the origin.

choices.value: The origin $O$ of the coordinate system
A point, different from the origin

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Curve Defined Parametrically With Trigonometric Functions
question.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\,\,y=-5\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t=\frac{x}{6} \\ y=-5\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{cos}⁡2t=-\frac{y}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using double angle formula for cosine and the Pythagorean identity, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t & ={cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =(1-{sin}^{2}⁡t)-{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{sin}⁡t=\frac{x}{6}$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡2t=-\frac{y}{5}$ into this formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{y}{5} & =1-2{(\frac{x}{6})}^{2} \\ -\frac{y}{5} & =1-2(\frac{{x}^{2}}{36}) \\ -\frac{y}{5} & =1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{18} \\ y & =-5+\frac{5{x}^{2}}{18}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=-5+\frac{5{x}^{2}}{18}.$

provenance.kp_title: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Curve Defined Parametrically With Trigonometric Functions

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Area Bounded by a Petal of a Polar Rose
question.problem: Which of the following gives the area bounded by the graph of the polar curve $r=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )$ for $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{4}?$
question.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )$, ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{4}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{3\pi }{4}$, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{3\pi /4}{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 9{\int }_{\pi /4}^{3\pi /4}{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{3\pi /4}{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the First Term Smaller Than a Given Value
question.problem:
What is the first term that is less than $0.000\,6$ in the following geometric sequence?

$$
64,\,32,\,16,\,8,\,…
$$
question.worked_solution:
The first term of the sequence is ${a}_{1}=64$ and the common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{32}{64}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =64\cdot {(\frac{1}{2})}^{n-1} \\  & ={2}^{6}\cdot {2}^{1-n} \\  & ={2}^{7-n}\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be less than $0.000\,6.$
Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & <0.000\,6 \\ {2}^{7-n} & <0.000\,6 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡{(2)}^{7-n} & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,6) \\ (7-n)\operatorname{log}⁡(2) & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,6) \\ 7-n & <\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,6)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)} \\ -n & <\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,6)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)}-7 \\ n & >7-\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,6)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get:

$$
7-\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,6)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)}≈17.703
$$

Therefore, the $18$th term is the first term of the sequence that is less than $0.000\,6.$

provenance.kp_title: Finding the First Term Smaller Than a Given Value

question.knowledge_point: Finding the First Term Smaller Than a Given Value
question.problem:
What is the first term that is less than $0.000\,08$ in the following geometric sequence?

$$
256,\,64,\,16,\,4,\,…
$$
question.worked_solution:
The first term of the sequence is ${a}_{1}=256$ and the common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{64}{256}=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =256\cdot {(\frac{1}{4})}^{n-1} \\  & ={4}^{4}\cdot {4}^{1-n} \\  & ={4}^{5-n}\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be less than $0.000\,08.$
Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & <0.000\,08 \\ {4}^{5-n} & <0.000\,08 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({4}^{5-n}) & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,08) \\ (5-n)\operatorname{log}⁡(4) & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,08) \\ 5-n & <\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,08)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(4)} \\ -n & <\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,08)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(4)}-5 \\ n & >5-\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,08)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(4)}\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get:

$$
5-\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,08)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(4)}≈11.805
$$

Therefore, the $12$th term is the first term of the sequence that is less than $0.000\,08.$

question.knowledge_point: Cases Where the First Term Is Unknown
question.problem:
The $6$th term of a geometric sequence is $3$, and the common ratio is $3.$ What is the first term of this sequence to exceed
$907?$
question.worked_solution:
Since we are given that ${a}_{6}=3$ and  $r=3$, we can use the $n$th term formula to solve for ${a}_{1}$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\ {a}_{6} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {3}^{6-1} \\ 3 & ={a}_{1}\cdot {3}^{5} \\ \frac{1}{{3}^{4}} & ={a}_{1} \\ {a}_{1} & =\frac{1}{81}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the $n$th term of the geometric sequence is

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{81}\cdot {3}^{n-1} \\  & ={3}^{-4}\cdot {3}^{n-1} \\  & ={3}^{n-5}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want $n$th term to be greater than $907.$
Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{n-5} & >907 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡{(3)}^{n-5} & >\operatorname{log}⁡(907) \\ (n-5)\operatorname{log}⁡(3) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(907) \\ n-5 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(907)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(3)} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(907)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(3)}+5\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get:

$$
\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(907)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(3)}+5≈11.199
$$

Therefore, the $12$th term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $907.$

provenance.kp_title: Cases Where the First Term Is Unknown

question.knowledge_point: Cases Where the First Term Is Unknown
question.problem:
The $3$rd term of a geometric sequence is $5$, and the $6$th term is $40.$ What is the first term of this sequence to exceed
$2\,020?$
question.worked_solution:
Since we are given that ${a}_{3}=5$ and ${a}_{6}=40$, we can find the common ratio $r$ of the sequence, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{n-m} & =\frac{{a}_{n}}{{a}_{m}} \\ {r}^{6-3} & =\frac{{a}_{6}}{{a}_{3}} \\ {r}^{3} & =\frac{40}{5} \\ {r}^{3} & =8 \\ r & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since ${a}_{3}=5$ and  $r=2$, we can use the $n$th term formula to solve for ${a}_{1}$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\ {a}_{3} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {2}^{3-1} \\ 5 & ={a}_{1}\cdot {2}^{2} \\ 5 & =4{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{1} & =\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the $n$th term of the geometric sequence is

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =\frac{5}{4}\cdot {2}^{n-1} \\  & =5\cdot \frac{1}{{2}^{2}}\cdot {2}^{n-1} \\  & =5\cdot {2}^{n-3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want $n$th term to be greater than $2\,020.$
Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}5\cdot {2}^{n-3} & >2\,020 \\ {2}^{n-3} & >404 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡{2}^{n-3} & >\operatorname{log}⁡(404) \\ (n-3)\operatorname{log}⁡(2) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(404) \\ n-3 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(404)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(404)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)}+3\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get:

$$
\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(404)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)}+3≈11.658
$$

Therefore, the $12$th term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $2\,020.$

provenance.kp_title: Cases Where the First Term Is Unknown

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Asymptotes of a Horizontal Hyperbola Given in Standard Form
question.problem: Calculate the asymptotes of the hyperbola $\frac{{x}^{2}}{16}-\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{9}=1.$
question.worked_solution:
The standard equation of a horizontal hyperbola centered at $(h,k)$ is

$$
\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

For a horizontal hyperbola, the equations of the asymptotes are

$$
y-k=\pm \frac{b}{a}(x-h).
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
(h,k)=(0,-2),\,a=\sqrt{16}=4,\,b=\sqrt{9}=3.
$$

 

Therefore, the asymptotes are given by

$$
y+2=\pm \frac{3}{4}x.
$$
